strengths: Novel and intuitive use of 3D Fourier basis functions for continuous video representation, with clear mathematical formulation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (Vid4, Adobe240, REDS) with extensive ablation studies demonstrating thorough investigation
Practical flexibility to handle arbitrary space-time scaling factors in a unified framework, unlike fixed-factor methods
Good empirical performance achieving >1dB improvement over VideoINR with better temporal consistency (lowest iOF score of 0.250)
Insightful analysis of learned basis functions and temporal consistency evaluation providing model interpretability
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty - essentially substitutes one continuous representation parameterization (INR) with another (Fourier basis) without demonstrating fundamental methodological advance over prior work
Unresolved critical limitation: acknowledged 'overly smooth' outputs at very high scaling factors with inadequate solutions or mitigation strategies
Contradicted efficiency claims: V³ inference time (1.27s) is actually longer than VideoINR baseline (3.03s reported), and VRAM usage comparisons are incomplete/incorrect in Table 5
Marginal empirical improvements: ~1-2 dB over baselines, which while consistent, do not represent transformative advances (e.g., 27.77 vs 27.64 PSNR over TTVSR in Table 7)
Incomplete baseline comparisons and missing recent SOTA methods; B-AVSR comparison unavailable 'at time of writing' severely undermines evaluation claims

Overclaimed simplicity and efficiency: 512 basis functions with learned frequencies/phases per voxel cell is not fundamentally simpler than VideoINR, and conditional parameterization adds substantial complexity
Lack of theoretical justification: no principled explanation for why Fourier basis is superior to other orthogonal bases (wavelets, Chebyshev polynomials) beyond intuition
Limited experimental scope: only low-resolution inputs (240p-1080p) and moderate upsampling (up to 8x); no evaluation on 4K inputs or extreme scaling factors
Weak ablation on model capacity: only tests basis functions up to N=768 without determining saturation point; insufficient evidence N=512 is sufficient

Inconsistent presentation: abstract and introduction make strong claims ('substantially improves', 'new state-of-the-art') not fully supported by 1dB experimental improvements and slower inference than baseline
Insufficient temporal consistency analysis: marginal iOF improvements (0.250 vs 0.254) and cherry-picked visual examples fail to strongly demonstrate advantage
No analysis of learned frequencies or failure mode characterization beyond oversmoothness; missing discussion of generalization across different video types

strengths: Novel Video Fourier Field (VFF) representation: An elegant, principled continuous spatio-temporal video model that naturally enables arbitrary-scale super-resolution without fixed factors
Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive evaluation across multiple tasks (C-STVSR, AVSR, VFI) and benchmarks (Vid4, GoPro, Adobe240, REDS) with consistent improvements >1 dB PSNR
Outperforms strong recent baselines: Beats BF-STVSR (2025) and other recent methods while using a smaller model (~14M parameters) and achieving superior temporal consistency
Thorough ablation studies and analysis: Includes basis function capacity analysis, learned function visualization (Figure 6), degradation robustness, and training sensitivity
Practical efficiency: Inference on consumer GPU (RTX 3050 Ti) with detailed computational analysis enabling accessibility
Versatile and unified framework: Naturally handles multiple upscaling factors, tasks, and both fixed and arbitrary-scale scenarios with strong temporal dynamics modeling
Clear mathematical formulation: Well-defined VFF representation with proper integration into encoder-decoder framework via conditional parameterization
Strong temporal consistency: Demonstrably better at capturing non-linear motion and handling temporal discontinuities than baselines
weaknesses: Framework novelty is incremental: While VFF representation is novel, the encoder-decoder integration is standard; the overall approach is representation replacement rather than architectural innovation
Incomplete baseline comparisons: AVSR comparison missing B-AVSR checkpoint at submission; some baselines dated (DAIN/EDVR 2018-2019), though recent baselines included
Limited theoretical justification: No rigorous proof for 'theoretically correct PSF' claim; missing analysis of frequency content representability versus spatial-domain methods

Generalization not demonstrated beyond standard benchmarks: No evaluation on extreme motion, very low quality inputs, variable frame rates/aspect ratios, or diverse degradation types beyond Gaussian noise and H.264

Hyperparameter choices lack thorough justification: 512 basis functions chosen with limited sensitivity analysis (Table 8 only tests 256/512/768); embedding dimensions (90, 12) appear arbitrary without ablation
Reproducibility concerns: No code availability mentioned; training computational cost not discussed; local voxel grid fitting details (Section 3.3) are unclear
Limited failure case analysis: Section 5 briefly mentions smoothness at high factors but provides minimal investigation; no discussion of content types or worst-case scenarios
Moderate empirical improvements: While consistent, ~1 dB PSNR gains are meaningful but not dramatic; doesn't represent fundamental breakthrough in field
Evaluation protocol questions: Doesn't discuss whether standard metrics are optimal for continuous methods; SSIM sensitivity to shifts may unfairly penalize continuous representations

Incomplete temporal motion analysis: While temporal consistency quantified, qualitative understanding of VFF's motion capture is limited; handling of accelerating/decelerating motion and periodic patterns not explored
